Decoding MT's Charts 7#

MT’s first entry was at the 1D BB, his stop simply covered the entire block. For this target, he chose an SR level in confluence with the equilibrium, marked with green circles.

For his second entry, he used the 1H BB that formed when price reversed at the 1D BB and led to a BOS. He entered at the lower edge of the BB and used the 1H BB below for stop placement.

His third entry becomes more interesting because PA initially front-ran the 2H BB he had marked. However, if you monitor higher timeframes, you’d notice that price had already taken liquidity by retesting the 12H OB (grey zone). 

It also took the OP, similar to how, in my previous decoding post, MT targeted the OP to avoid getting front-run.  

MT likely entered around the fib he marked, covering the entire BB with his stop in case PA tried to grab that liquidity as well. For his TP, he chose the SR level and a 12H OB in confluence with the HTF EQ (Image 1).
In his post, MT also mentioned that he moved his stop up. This was probably due to price reaching the EQ of the previous swing, which he also often uses for his first TP.

Laddering of TFs.

HTF Fuel > MTF Fuel > LTF entry.

You can always use lower TF levels to either add size or de-risk by trailing your stop behind them.

Price is constantly bouncing from one level to the next.

text:
How to maximize your returns?

Don’t just chase higher risk-reward ratios, focus on the probability of your stop being hit.

You have to think in expected values rather than absolute RR.

A 1 to 10 RR with a wide stop isn’t necessarily worse than a 1 to 20 RR setup with a tight stop.

The tighter your stop, the faster your hit rate decreases, and it doesn’t decrease linearly but exponentially due to the inherent variance of the market.

Instead, think in expected values: 

Expected value = (Reward × Hitrate) - (Loss × (1 - Hitrate) )

Consider these scenarios:  
10R with a 60% hit rate is not equivalent to 20R with a 30% hit rate.

Expected value calculations:
10* 0.6 - 1 * 0.4 = 5.6
20* 0.3 - 1* 0.7 = 5.3

Don’t maximize risk-reward. Maximize expected value.

Expected value is the only metric that matters if you want to maximize your earnings over time.

The law of large numbers ensures returns move toward the expected value.

text:
💡Why Breakerblocks work? 

Market makers (MMs) and institutions often use iceberg orders to hide their size. Imagine it like an algorithm that wants to sell 1 million but starts by selling 10k every minute. 

Their main job is to create the necessary counterparty liquidity within that area, either by continuously stopping out retail traders through Wyckoff, 3-Drive, or Head & Shoulders patterns, or by using forced liquidations. 

That’s why price often starts distributing within order blocks (OBs). It’s a mechanism to bait retail into opening positions into their iceberg orders.  

However, once MMs decide there’s more to gain from going higher, they simply push through the area of the iceberg algorithm. If the algo is meant to distribute 1 million but is only selling 10k a minute, most of the liquidity will stay intact if the price pushes through fast enough.  

Now, if price pushes through and leads to a break of structure, it means MMs aren’t interested in the liquidity that a swing failure pattern (SFP) might provide to fill their shorts, they show intention to push higher.  

If price retraces back into the previously ignored area of the iceberg algorithm, it activates again after price enters the BB. 

The main misconception is that bullish BBs don’t provide buying pressure. 

They provide the opportunity of counterparty liquidity that MMs can use to fill their new capital injections, using the sell volume to fill their longs. In essence, they are converting or recycling old orders to align with their new intentions.

That’s also how SFPs work: they don’t create buy volume at a bottom. They create sell volume that MMs can use to fill their orders.  

Only OBs themselves add buying or selling pressure due to unfilled orders from the past.

That’s just a theory. I’m open to your suggestions or improvements.

text:
Market Algorithms vs. The EMH Myth

The Efficient Market Hypothesis is taught everywhere in universities, but even Jim Simons, the founder of the most successful quant fund, says it’s wrong. 

Markets are irrational because their participants, like retail, are emotional. This irrationality is exactly what the algos exploit. They see it as an illogical anomaly and execute to maximize its exploitation.

However, even the most sophisticated bots are limited by available liquidity to exploit an edge.
 
This is exactly why Renaissance Technologies never accepted unlimited capital. They knew their models couldn't be executed with that much size without destroying the edge.

Every algo is balancing multiple variables:

How big is the statistical edge?

How much capital can exploit it before it breaks?

How can counterparty capital be maximized (often through news, wyckoff)?

What proprietary data inputs/insider information do I have that the public doesn't?

These players aren't interested in exploiting an edge immediately, they want to exploit it to the maximum. 

They do this by baiting all other participants to misposition themselves, providing the smart money with the cheapest and largest fill for their massive orders.

They are machines fed with insider information to position MMs at the most advantageous position  before this information takes effect.

text:
What did MT mean with VSA analysis?

Imagine the entire market as a massive order book (DOM) filled with limit orders of different sizes at different prices.

Movement between these levels is lead by the delta of market orders. If market orders are strong enough, they absorb the limit orders and push to the next price level until for example buyers are exhausted, allowing sellers to take over and push through the limit orders below. It is a constant game of ping-pong between these limits/liquidity.

It is widely assumed that market makers use mostly limit orders to avoid slippage and lower transaction fees. While heatmaps can visualize this liquidity, the data is often manipulative. 

Limit orders are often cancelled moments before the price touches them, also known as spoofing.

If market makers decide to pull their limit orders, the price will dump until it hits a new wall of liquidity below that begins absorbing the market selling. (e.g. Oct 10)

Market makers sometimes increase liquidity (limit orders) at certain Key Levels while market orders attempt to push through without success. This creates CVD divergences, which are basically the same as the VSA analysis MT once mentioned. It signals MM involvement and the absorption of retail orders by them.

Images by @goldenpocketxbt
author: OverlordEins

text:
Important:

CVD = Cumulative Volume Delta. 

It shows the development of the sum of the deltas (buy market orders − sell market orders) across consecutive candles. 

Let’s say it starts at 0 and the next candle has a delta of −50. Then the CVD decreases by 50, so the new CVD is −50. If the next candle’s delta is −10, the CVD decreases again, from −50 to −60.

text:
⚠️ Why do visual candlestick patterns like OB/BBs even work? 

To understand the logic behind these, one must understand how volume is created within a chart. 

In the past, before retail traders had access to precise volume data, Time Price Opportunity (TPO) charts were used to approximate volume. 

For volume to occur, price needs to be present. Volume then shows the participation in trade at those levels. 

The presence of price and the time spent there is a limiting factor for Market Makers to get their large orders filled. The less time spent at a level, the less participation (volume) is possible. 

Looking at an example of an extended TPO profile, one can notice that it closely imitates a 30-minute candlestick chart, simply without any wicks.

Now, to approximate the volume at different prices, these 30-minute candles are added up horizontally to create a profile. 

Using this profile, one can identify where price spent most of its time and probably transacted most of its volume. Looking at the image below, one can clearly see the overlap between the TPO Profile (blue/white) on the left and the Volume Profile on the right.

The TPO profile also shows where price spent the least amount of time through single prints. 

These are areas where, by adding up all blocks horizontally, there is only one block in width. Those are often either wicks (tails = 3 single prints) or FVGs that are commonly used as S/R levels. (last image)

So, why do candlestick patterns even work? 
When we use them, we are essentially doing the same thing as analyzing a profile: we are identifying areas where many time-blocks overlap.

That is why MT also focuses mainly on the candle body rather than the wicks. A basic OB on a HTF shows a summary of multiple low-TF candle bodies that spent a lot of time within that area. 

This presence at a price level is often created by MMs trying to fill large orders, which translates directly into volume. A BB is similar, except that price previously spent a lot of time forming an OB, which then gets ignored by printing single prints/FVG. Similarly, refining works on the same principle by narrowing it down to the highest density of bodies.

The last image is from @luckychartape's discord. He made it free for this week. I would recommend joining to check it out, he even made a video on this topic.

Volume simply means retail and MMs are matching their orders, but retail is usually mispositioned. Once in a trending market, price retests those areas; retail exits at Break Even while MMs might add size. After those retail traders have exited at BE, the effect of the next touch will be lower, similar to how KL become weaker after multiple touches. 

FVGs work well with Single Prints, but without liquidity behind them, they aren't as powerful.

text:
⚠️ How to Filter Out Weak Order Blocks

In the past, I compared OB/BB to a Time Price Opportunity chart. If we know that price spent six months within a very small range, we can approximate where most of the liquidity is located. 

Image 1:
However, with an OB where the wicks are disproportionately larger than the order block itself, using only the candle body might distort that. The wicks show the wide range in which price spent those six months. If we choose the candle body as a key liquidity level, the chance that the volume is actually in the wicks increases.

Image 2: 
On the other hand, if we go down to the 5 month timeframe, we might see an order block with almost no wicks. When there are very small wicks, we can be more confident that most liquidity is concentrated within the body of the candle. In that case, we know that price spent roughly five months within that narrow range.  

Observing how price reacted, the 5 month block seemed to work better. In MTC, we might describe this as price taking all the liquidity hidden in the wicks.

That’s also why order blocks tend to work better when they align with the POC — because that alignment might correct for any distortions caused by wick extremes.

When refining order blocks, we also check multiple timeframes to find overlapping levels that confirm that price spent the most time within a specific range, which increases the probability of it being a key market maker zone.

It’s just a theory I’m still working on, but I wanted to share my current thoughts.

What do you think of this theory? 

I haven’t done enough backtesting yet, but from a logical standpoint, it seems to make sense. 

Of course, candle closes themselves also show institutional bias, and MT also says that volume is located within the body.

However, he then also refines the wicks into bodies, choosing the areas where most of them overlap.

text:
⚠️ Bojan Highs/Lows

Represent lower TF Wyckoff Models.

Model 1 Bojan: Summarizes the two deviations of the lower timeframe Wyckoff M1 (Image 1)
Model 2 Bojan: Similar structure, but the third wick does not deviate beyond the second, comparable to a Wyckoff M2. (Image 2)

High Probability Bojans:
1.Ranging environment: If we ignore the wicks, candle bodies aren't in a trend. (see #2)
 
2. The second candle’s close is approximately at the same level as the first candle’s close, showing that the deviation's intent was to only hunt stops. Similarily, the third candle's close should be close to the second candle's.

3.Ideally, the lows aren't deviated (swept) by the following candles' lows, which could be beneficial for a stronger reversal. (Unswept highs for bullish Bojans) => RTZ

You can find them very often within Key Liquidity. There are many variations, and they don’t necessarily need to form in textbook-perfect conditions if your level is high probability.

Entry with Bojans is at the third candle close. SL at the Swing Low/SH of the third candle.

Example: 1W candle close above Key Liquidity + aligns with candle close of Model 2 Bojan.

Shortcut: Finding Orderblocks/FVGs on different timeframes

Merge consecutive candles of the same color before an opposite-color FVG formation into one candle.

It’s a useful concept to start merging candles in your head, because that’s basically what happens when you switch timeframes.

The formation of an (MTF) FVG on the lower TF gives us more confidence that market makers are involved.

A higher timeframe FVG forms when a lower timeframe FVG is not mitigated by the candles on either side. The farther outward you can move without price wicking into the full FVG, the higher the FVG’s implied timeframe.

Using this you can also find orderblocks that can't be seen on higher TFs due to different anchor times.

text:
Order Block Blueprint

There are different levels of strength to them.

Validation: The green candle body is bigger than the red candle body.

Strength criteria:
1. Close above the previous candle’s (wick) high, indicating a BOS on the lower timeframe.

2. Break of structure confirming a trend change.

3. FVG formation, giving confidence in market maker involvement.

Additional criteria:
1. Formed during an SFP or within a higher-timeframe liquidity block.
(+ Internal sweep before OB formation.
This makes the OB similar to a Wyckoff Model 2)

2. Range Extreme: Extreme Discount/Premium

3. Refinable: We want as many bodies—and therefore as much volume—as possible to overlap within our higher-timeframe OB zone. Wicks should be smaller relative to the candle body because they can hide lower-timeframe candle bodies.

Institutional trading volume is concentrated at the bodies. Wicks can many times be printed in 1 second.
author: OverlordEins

text:
Why do we refine?

Refinable means that we go through different timeframes to identify Orderblocks on them too.

Volume is usually within the candle bodies rather than the wicks.
 
Wicks can happen within seconds, but on higher timeframes this doesn't always have to apply.

If we find a monthly Orderblock which, when we try to refine it, shows that most bodies are within the wick, then our thesis of liquidity being within the Monthly Orderblock isn't confirmed.

Imagine it like this: price starts at 1 at the start of the month, jumps up to 10 on the second day, spends the whole month there, but shortly before the close it drops, let's say, to 2.

PA on the monthly would show a candle body between 1 and 2, while the PA above would be shown as a wick.

So refining basically means simply confirming where price spent its time.

Different timeframes will show different closes. When we go on the weekly and see that most bodies are within the wick, the monthly is clearly invalidated. But then we can check where within those weekly levels most bodies, and therefore liquidity, might be located.

As MT says, "Institutional trading volume is concentrated at the bodies." We are simply double-checking by refining to avoid anomalies.

I will probably make a more detailed post in the future with some decent graphics.

I hope this helped you in your understanding.

Ask follow up questions if something is unclear.

I am always grateful for some feedback so I can improve my explanations in the future and check where I might have gaps in my own understanding.

It’s an abbreviation for “draw on liquidity.”

Anything that can serve as the next logical liquidity pool for market makers to rebalance their inventory. They earn the spread by providing liquidity. However, at the extremes of a range, they must act as the counterparty to massive liquidation spikes. During those periods, their inventory can become overexposed to one side. To avoid that risk, price draws to the other side of liquidity so they can rebalance. That happens on all timeframes, higher timeframe once carry simply more liquidity. 

DOL Examples: SL/SH, especially equal lows and equal highs, because more stops are usually located below or above them. FVGs above those SL/SH levels may get filled during the same move. It’s even better if there are BBs behind those FVGs or OBs above those SH/SL levels.

⚠️ Decoding Moneytaur ⚠️

The BCHUSDT chart was chosen.

🔸The setup idea was to trade a breakout into the Monthly Partial Breakerblock at 520.

🔸As a primary continuation level, one can use the MTF (11H + 2H + ...) order blocks. However, to increase the RR, rather than targeting the MTF OB itself, one can target potential price wicks into the LTF OB below, within the MTF wick.

🔸Going into the lower timeframe, the first LTF order block is a 15 minute order block.

🔸To refine it even further, one can go into the timeframes between 2 and 7 minutes to find order blocks hidden between two FVGs. This refined level also aligns perfectly with the previous S/R level and is nearby the EQ of the 15-minute order block.

🔸Now, some might ask why MT would long a level in premium. When looking at confluence charts, such as the BCHBTC chart, one can see that price was within a 2M order block during this breakout. He probably used this as additional confluence for the breakout.

Depends on the timeframe and strength of the level you trade.

If it's only a MTF Level you shouldn't use the 0,5 of a very large HTF swing. The level simply doesn't have enough fuel and will probably retrace to take more without you capitalizing on the swing.

Also check if those TP targets align with good levels. If there isn't much in the way on those timeframes like Swing Highs/Lows and OB/BB you might consider a bigger swing.

If many majors align the expansion will be stronger and you anticipate that and TP wider on bigger swings.

A good example is the recent pump on altcoins but with BTC at a bearish WBB(+POC of previous range) refined into 12H OB. One would TP earlier or hedge on BTC.

Also if you have hedges running on other coins you might want to keep the positions running longer. But you have to consider that ALTs are basically positions on BTC with leverage. Check also ALT/BTC pairs to see which pair will probably outperform BTC to know which one to use as hedge.

Simply try to assume where is it reasonable that price will go against me. That's what the 0,5 fib (0,618) rule is about. Because the 0,5 fib usually gets hit before continuation. 

If it gets hit and respected price is probably still trending against you and the Level it bounced from was just an obstacle in its path that got absorbed before continuation.

Simply try to have two perspectives on the set up where will it go against me in the bearish scenario and where will it go to in a bullish scenario. That's also why one TPs there to secure profits before a potential bearish scenario may form. You position for both.

text:
I see breaker blocks from an orderflow perspective as a zone of trapped traders. The FVG itself shows that price moved through the OB, giving those traders not much time to exit. 

There could also be traders that try to double done at the OB at the first retest (can usually be seen by lower TF OB closer to the FVG) but get offside when the FVG moves through so a FVG provides multiple opportunities for traders to get offside and later be used as counterparty.

Now when price returns to that area those traders can finally exit at BE and provide the fill to bigger players betting on continuation. I picture OB as High Volume Nodes that get revisited to provide a counterparty an entry/exit if they get ignored someone didn't want to use them for that purpose but when moving through the other side within the OB gets into negative PNL and after a restest closes to exit at BE. That's how Breakerblocks switch between bullish and bearish.  However price also often wicks into OBs nearby so everything depends on how big the player wants to get filled.

Then FVGs themselves are also areas at which players that wanted to get filled got skipped during the move and now get another chance to jump into the trend. It might also provide an opportunity for market makers to rebalance at the lows of the newly formed ranged and rebalance the inventory that they had to absorb during the move up. 

I am still digging especially the FVG part itself is very ambigious at the moment it's just a theory I try to build around it based on all the players incentives. 

My assumption is simply that candle sticks approximate a footprint chart and I try to translate those orderflow concepts into Price Action trading.

🧵My Simplified Version of Ranges and Wyckoff

I usually don’t take ranges that seriously.

For me, it is rather simple market structure that defines my range.

In an uptrend, you’re basically seeing continuously new ranges being created, or price going sideways, deviating, and retesting previous ranges, or deviating the new SH/SL.

Most rules make it too difficult and distracting.

I’d rather simplify it down to the basic mechanics behind it: stops getting hunted (SFP) and supply and demand, like order blocks and (n)POC, being retested.

For me, Wyckoff doesn’t need to be unnecessarily complex.

I simply trade either the SFP or the retest of an OB formed during an SFP, or similar cases. That’s usually the logic that forms the Wyckoff pattern on the chart.

I don’t limit myself to a narrow framework. I mostly just observe the reaction within my level to decide whether I should enter.

That’s all you really need to know about Wyckoff. It’s basically the interaction of stop hunts, order blocks, and market structure.

I don’t really care if it fits the textbook definition of Wyckoff. I simply trade the market structure range, whether we are trending or ranging. 

This is at least my own approach to it, that works for me.

If something was unclear, leave a comment.

text:
With alts I look often at the ALT/BTC chart to see which one is more probable to outperform. They can be very useful to decide which asset to use for hedges.

However BTC should always be prioritized. If BTC is at supply and starts selling off Alts will follow in most cases. There can be exceptions, if there are aggressive positions in those alts that will first get squeezed. The levels can give small reactions but not very big profits so one has to be very careful trading against BTC's trend.

My approach is to simply put BTC first and then use alts if they align. Because they are mostly leveraged positions of BTC.

Back to your example where BTC is at 1H supply but 4H Demand.

In this case I would monitor BTC for its MS and how price acts around the 1H resistance if I see it holding market structure, trendlines holding and order flow is convincing for a breakout. 

Then I might attempt a tight long on the altcoin even if it is in a range. Because it might be an assymentrical bet on a breakout. I might  simply attempt it as a small scalp of the 1H support that might develop into a swing if all conditions align.

However one has to be able to adapt fast and trail stops and TP1 just in case. It might become more difficult. Try to first trade BTC profitably and only then add Altcoins on top.

quote.text:
For spot & futures traders/investors. For anyone who wants to take their game to the next level and gradually begin outperforming the market 👇

HTF plays > up to 3% of trading account (max 5% if optimal). These optimal plays is where the big gains are, and you run them for weeks to months while playing shorter-term opportunities, and if any of your shorter-term plays goes against your expectation, you "shave off" some profit from your HTF play in order to cover that smaller loss. It's called: Hedging (Risk management). Always strive to be in such plays, whether in Futures or Spot trading.

MTF plays > up to 2% of trading account. These trades can last several days to few weeks. 

LTF plays > up to 1% of trading account. These plays can last minutes, hours, or 2-3 days. There's more "noise" here, and volatility. Not the wisest trading style for inexperienced traders, and in a market that's open 24/7 with thousands of different coins, there's no need to chase what most assume to be "fast
quote.author: Moneytaur_

⚠️ RANGES ⚠️

You can identify a range when the PA of an asset moves sideways between a SH and SL. PA will continue to play in that range until a SH or SL is broken. Once broken, assume PA to pull back into the range and reverse for continuation into the broken SH or SL https://t.co/6eUSveVuoG
author: CryptoChase02

quote.text:
NEGATIVE FIBONNACCI RETRACEMENT

Sometimes you won't have data (Previous PA) to help you out with where the price could potentially react. Place the start of your fib from PSL (previous swing low) to PSH (previous swing high). It will then show you above where the price could react. Now if you want to find levels below (finding the bottom) then you just do the opposite of what I said above.

It will most likely be a general area and not react exactly off the fib level.

quote.text:
FIBONACCI RETRACEMENT 

Firstly, who cares about the definition we just want to know how to use it effectively. The numbers you need to know are:
- 0.5
- 0.618
- 0.705
- 0.786
- -0.5
- -0.618

The most important fib level is 0.5 as it is the "equilibrium", not the "golden pocket" (Retail mindset)

Understand that the other fib levels are not better than each other. How you should proceed to look at them is that fib levels will line up with where key liquidity areas are due to be taken. 

Placing the start of the fib level from SL to SH (Down to Up) will show you support levels. Placing the start of the fib level from SH to SL (Up to Down) will show you resistance levels.

Here's the secret, sometimes you'll need to measure the swings. It will show you an untested fib level. They are just as important as they show you liquidity in that area hasn't been tapped yet.

quote.text:
⚠️ RISK MANAGEMENT ⚠️

Firstly, understand HTF > MTF > LTF

You will make more money risking the HTF plays than the MTF/LTF plays and they are more favourable.

How to calculate position size: 

(Risk / Stop loss) x 100

For example: $100 account with 2% risk and my stop loss is 5% away 

$100 x 0.02 = $2 
$2 / 5 = 0.4 
0.4 x 100 = $40 
The position size should be $40 

This is the way I calculate and this method has helped me to manage my risk effectively.

This is my most frequently used setup for opening momentum (MO) positions, typically on the 5-15 minute chart with a focus on SFP (Swing Failure Pattern). For optimal effectiveness, the price must align with a higher timeframe key level—otherwise, it’s treated as a scalp trade.

The setup occurs when price crosses a recent swing high or low but swiftly retraces below or above that level without the candlestick body closing beyond it. This move creates a clear invalidation point (ideal for stop-loss placement) and offers an excellent risk-to-reward (R:R) ratio.

In most cases, especially after a prolonged uptrend, the price doesn’t usually reverse immediately upon its first touch of a resistance level. Instead, it often performs an SFP, delivering a second approach to the same level. This behavior is rooted in market psychology—before a trend reversal, price often needs to "equalize" or balance liquidity at key levels.

You can identify a range when the PA of an asset moves sideways between a SH and SL. PA will continue to play in that range until a SH or SL is broken. Once broken, assume PA to pull back into the range and reverse for continuation into the broken SH or SL direction.

MMs and algorithms will always play the game within a range until broken as they will buy/long in the discount zone and sell/short in the premium zone.

⚠️ FAIR VALUE GAPS ⚠️

A fair value gap (FVG) occurs when PA shows a price imbalance or inefficiency. It typically occurs when PA moves fast in one direction (aggressive buying/selling), leaving little to no trading activity or liquidity at certain price levels. This gap can also hide key levels from retail players. FVGs show institutional involvement, so it's good to know how to use them, as you will play alongside the 🐳's entering at key levels.

Knowing the importance of how FVGs are supposed to be played will increase your success massively.

FVGs are also known as displacements and imbalances. Just different terms used.

Always look for untested FVGs rather than FVGs that have already been mitigated as they are more powerful, especially with key liquidity behind them. Touched FVGs become less valid as they have already been tested. The more tests, the less valid. 

The more FVGs there are, the harder it becomes to see key liquidity as they are more hidden. The more hidden, the mor

The Fibonacci extensions 1.272, 1.454, and 1.618 levels play a crucial role in my technical approach, not only for
identifying levels in price discovery, but also on intra-swing setups.

Why?

Because they often align with deeper principles of market structure and smart money concepts.

As you can see from the INJ example I posted, when we draw an extension from a significant internal or external swing say from point A to B in a corrective leg or impulsive move, we're essentially mapping out where smart money may be targeting liquidity or where their orders might be getting filled.

⚠️ STOP LOSS ⚠️

A stop loss (SL) is used to limit losses and manage risk. If PA moves against your desired direction and your SL is hit, your position will automatically close, protecting your capital from rapidly decreasing. Using a SL will allow you to focus on other trades without the worry of your current trade. 

If your SL is hit, it doesn't mean you were wrong; the probabilities were against you. Anything can happen in this market, and you have to be ready for multiple scenarios.

SL acts as a pillar for your risk management. Without a SL, your risk management will be terrible. Read about my risk management post here 👉 https://t.co/OKJmqTkfrv

One place to put your SL is underneath the key level that you identified. The higher the volume on your chosen coin, the more likely your key level will be respected (Focus on higher R/R + Smaller SL).

quote.text:
Orderflow CVD:

• CVD tracks aggressive Buyer/Sellers(Market Orders)

It doesn't track limit orders that are executed at the CMP.

• If Price declines + CVD rises => Market Orders(Retail) are buying into the Supply of MM (limit orders)

• If Price increases + CVD declines =>Market Orders(Retail) are selling into the Demand of MM.

• When Price tests a KL and a divergence forms
=> Limit Orders of MM are getting filled

It helps to identify if there are Shorts opening=>possible Short Squeeze

• CVD increases: Opening Longs or Closing Shorts

• CVD decreases: Closing Longs or Opening Shorts.

Open Interest(OI)
• OI +1 when Long opens + Short opens
• OI -1 when Long closes + Short closes

Combine both: CVD + OI

CVD decreases + OI increase = Shorts opening

CVD increases + OI increases = Longs opening

🧵 TCT Blueprint

author: OverlordEins

text:
Market Structure: 6 candle rule
-Two consecutive candles of same colour
-the second candle has to be either lower or higher than the previous one.
-the structure is invalid when the second candle is within the wicks of the previous one

Image 2:
Green⬆️ not valid
Red    ⬇️ valid https://t.co/4nPD2BkedM
author: OverlordEins

text:
BOS: 

• Good BOS: Not only candle close above SH/SL

BUT also second candle closes above SH/SL

• Bad BOS: Second candle retraces back. =>Wick on higher TF

• Domino Effect:
LTF BOS > MTF BOS > HTF BOS https://t.co/IsGluUCm8Y
author: OverlordEins

text:
If PA wicks above the SH and retraces (=SFP) the BOS high is updated to the SFP SH.

However if PA SFP/wicks above previous SH and the next candle pushes through the BOS high stays the same(PSH).

Examples 2/3 https://t.co/VZQJCaO5fY
author: OverlordEins

text:
OBIF, Structural S&D

OBIF: OB with Inefficiency = FVG
• 3 candle formation: 
Candle of Opposite colour > Expansion > Third candle wick confirmes valid FVG

Structural S&D: You include all the candles which are below the FVG.

=>Sign of Market Maker involvement https://t.co/n5O1XUW94I
author: OverlordEins

text:
Trendline and Curve Liquidity.

Liquidity = Where the most Stop Losses are located

Most Stops are located above SH/below SL

Buy Side Liquidity = Short Stops
Sell Side Liquidity = Long Stops
author: OverlordEins

text:
Trendlines are used by MM to fill their positions.

Every consecutive lower high that retraces from a Trendline aggregates stops placed above 
+ stops that are trailed.

A TL works only as long until MM decide to fill their positions. https://t.co/B4XdQIOerS
author: OverlordEins

• Level taken not just small wick

LTF S&D
• Refine LTF PA within/close to Key Level into OB/BB
